sections.heading: The Mughal Empire — India's grand imperial state

blocks.text: The **Mughal Empire (1526–1857)** — founded by **Babur** (Panipat 1526) — became **medieval India's most integrated, prosperous and culturally luminous state**. The **Great Mughals** — **Babur, Humayun, Akbar (1556–1605, the architect of the system), Jahangir, Shah Jahan (the golden age of art), Aurangzeb (greatest extent, then decline)** — built an administration so durable that even the British inherited its vocabulary (mansab, jagir, subah, diwan).

rows: **Central administration**
The **Emperor** at apex; four ministries — **Diwan (finance), Mir Bakhshi (military/mansab), Sadr (religion/charity), Mir Saman (household)**; a centralised, Persianised bureaucracy.
**Mansabdari system**
**Akbar's** ranking of nobles by **zat (personal rank) & sawar (cavalry)** — a graded, transferable, salaried service nobility; the empire's steel frame; paid via **jagir** (revenue assignments).
**Land revenue — Zabti/Dahsala**
**Todar Mal's** settlement — measured land, classified soil, fixed a cash demand (~1/3 produce) on a ten-year average; the fiscal engine that funded everything.
**Provincial**
**Subah (province) → Sarkar → Pargana → village**; **Subedar (governor), Diwan (revenue), Faujdar (law-order)** — a replicable pyramid.

sections.heading: Socio-religious life & culture — the Ganga-Jamuni synthesis

items: **Religious policy — the great arc**: **Akbar's** liberal synthesis — abolition of jizya (1564), **Sulh-i-kul (universal peace), Din-i-Ilahi, Ibadat Khana debates, Rajput alliances** — versus **Aurangzeb's** orthodoxy (jizya re-imposed 1679, temple friction) — the swing of policy is the empire's central socio-religious debate; present both with balance.

**Art & architecture — the golden age**: **Indo-Islamic-Persian fusion** at its zenith — **Fatehpur Sikri, Humayun's Tomb, the Taj Mahal, Red Fort, Jama Masjid**; **charbagh gardens, pietra dura, the bulbous dome & pishtaq**; Mughal **miniature painting** (Persian + Indian schools).

**Literature & language**: **Persian** the court language (Abul Fazl's Ain-i-Akbari & Akbarnama); **Urdu's flowering**; translations of Sanskrit epics; the **Bhakti-Sufi** currents (HCOI-018) continuing beneath.

**Economy & society**: a **monetised, trade-rich economy** (textiles, the silver influx, karkhanas, flourishing towns — Ibn-era travellers marvel); a hierarchical society of nobility, zamindars, artisans and peasantry; women's seclusion alongside powerful figures (Nur Jahan).

sections.heading: Shivaji and the rise of the Marathas

blocks.text: **Shivaji (1630–1680)** carved a **sovereign Maratha state** out of the Deccan against both the **Bijapur Sultanate and Mughal power**, crowning himself **Chhatrapati at Raigad (1674)**. He fused **guerrilla warfare (ganimi kava), a hill-fort network, naval power and an efficient revenue-military administration** into the **first durable indigenous challenge to Mughal supremacy** — the seed of the 18th-century Maratha confederacy that would dominate India.

rows: **Ashta Pradhan**
A council of **eight ministers** — Peshwa (PM), Amatya, Mantri, Sachiv, Sumant, Senapati, Panditrao, Nyayadhish; a merit bureaucracy, offices non-hereditary.
**Revenue**
**Chauth (1/4) & Sardeshmukhi (1/10)** — levies on neighbouring territories; land assessed on measurement; cash salaries curbed jagir-style feudalism.
**Military & forts**
**Guerrilla warfare (ganimi kava)**, a light mobile cavalry, and a chain of **hill forts** (Raigad, Pratapgarh, Sinhagad); a paid standing army over feudal levies.
**Navy**
A pioneering **Maratha navy** guarding the Konkan coast — forts at Sindhudurg, Vijaydurg — earning Shivaji the 'father of the Indian navy' epithet.

sections.heading: From Shivaji to empire — the confederacy

items: **Shivaji's method**: religious tolerance (protected mosques, employed Muslims), a Marathi-Sanskrit cultural revival, and a state resting on **Deccan peasant support** rather than a narrow nobility — a genuinely **regional, popular kingship**.

**Sambhaji, Rajaram, Tarabai**: the state survived a **27-year war with Aurangzeb (1681–1707)** — Aurangzeb died in the Deccan, the war that drained and doomed the Mughals; Maratha resilience is the story of Mughal decline (HCOI-021).

**The Peshwa era**: under the **Peshwas (Balaji Vishwanath, Baji Rao I, Balaji Baji Rao)** the state became a **confederacy** — Scindias (Gwalior), Holkars (Indore), Gaekwads (Baroda), Bhonsles (Nagpur) — expanding to Delhi and Attock.

**The check — Panipat 1761**: the crushing defeat by **Ahmad Shah Abdali** halted Maratha northward expansion; recovery under Madhav Rao followed, but the confederacy's decentralisation left it vulnerable to the **British (Anglo-Maratha Wars, 1775–1818)**.

sections.heading: The advent of the Europeans — the race for Indian trade

blocks.text: The **European arrival (1498–1757)** began with **Vasco da Gama reaching Calicut (1498)** and unfolded as a **century-long commercial contest** among the **Portuguese, Dutch, English, French and Danes** for India's fabled trade — spices, textiles, indigo, saltpetre. What began as **seaborne commerce ended as territorial empire**: the trading companies, drawn into Indian politics amid Mughal decline, became rulers.

rows: **Portuguese (1498)**
First and last to leave; **Goa (1510, Albuquerque), Daman, Diu**; monopoly via the **cartaz** pass system & Estado da India; declined by 1600s but held Goa till 1961.
**Dutch (1602, VOC)**
Focused on the **spice islands** (Indonesia); Indian bases at Pulicat, Nagapattinam; ousted from India after **Bedara (1759)**; dominant in textiles briefly.
**English (1600, EIC)**
**Surat (1613), Madras (1639), Bombay (1668), Calcutta (1690)**; won the long game via naval-financial strength and Plassey (1757).
**French (1664, CIO)**
**Pondicherry, Chandernagore, Mahe**; **Dupleix** nearly won the Carnatic; lost the Anglo-French **Carnatic Wars (1746-63)**, sealed at Wandiwash (1760).

sections.heading: Trade practices — how commerce became conquest

items: **The commodity draw**: Europe craved **Indian textiles (calico, muslin), spices (pepper), indigo, saltpetre and silk**, paying largely in **bullion (silver)** — India ran a huge trade surplus; the 'drain' would reverse only under British rule (HCOI-024).

**The company form**: **joint-stock chartered companies** (EIC 1600, VOC 1602) with **royal monopolies, private armies and the right to make war/peace** — a novel fusion of commerce and sovereignty that let them act as states.
**Fortified factories**: walled trading posts (factories) at coastal sites, evolving into **garrisoned forts** (Fort St. George, Fort William) — the nuclei of later territorial power.

**The Carnatic Wars (the turning point)**: Anglo-French rivalry, fought through **subsidiary alliances with Indian rulers**, showed that **European-trained sepoy armies could decide Indian successions** — the template Clive would use at Plassey; the AP/Coromandel coast was the crucible (Dupleix at Pondicherry).

sections.heading: The rise of the East India Company's hegemony

blocks.text: Between **Plassey (1757) and the Charter Act of 1833**, a **trading company became the sovereign of India**. Exploiting **Mughal decline and regional rivalries**, the **English East India Company** converted commercial dominance into **territorial paramountcy** through **decisive battles, the Diwani, subsidiary alliances and outright annexation** — an empire acquired, in Seeley's phrase, almost 'in a fit of absence of mind', but in truth by systematic method.

rows: **Plassey (1757)**
**Clive** defeated **Siraj-ud-Daulah** of Bengal via conspiracy (Mir Jafar); the Company gained control of the richest province — the financial base of empire.
Defeat of the combined **Mughal-Awadh-Bengal** forces; **1765 Diwani** of Bengal-Bihar-Orissa gave the Company revenue rights — legal sovereignty over Bengal.
**Subsidiary Alliance (Wellesley)**
Indian rulers hosted (and paid for) Company troops, surrendered foreign relations — **Hyderabad, Awadh, Marathas** drawn in; expansion without direct war.
**Doctrine of Lapse (Dalhousie)**
States without a natural heir 'lapsed' to the Company — **Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur, Awadh (misgovernance)** annexed; a grievance feeding 1857.

items: **Military-fiscal engine**: the **Diwani** let the Company fund its army from Bengal's revenues and buy Indian goods with Indian taxes — the beginning of the **'drain of wealth'** (Dadabhai Naoroji) that reversed India's old trade surplus.

**Political method — three tools**: **outright war/annexation** (Mysore against Tipu 1799, the Anglo-Maratha & Anglo-Sikh Wars), **Subsidiary Alliances** (Wellesley), and the **Doctrine of Lapse** (Dalhousie) — war, diplomacy and legal fiction combined.

**Administrative consolidation**: Parliament's growing control via the **Regulating Act (1773), Pitt's India Act (1784), and the Charter Acts (1813 ended trade monopoly, 1833 made the Governor-General of India supreme)** — the Company governed as an agent of the Crown.

**Economic transformation**: **deindustrialisation** of Indian textiles, commercialisation of agriculture, new land-revenue systems (Permanent Settlement 1793, Ryotwari, Mahalwari — HCOI-025), and the drain — the material roots of the freedom struggle.

sections.heading: Colonial change — administration, society and culture remade

blocks.text: British rule did not merely change India's rulers — it **restructured the state, the economy and social life**. A **centralised bureaucratic administration, Western education, new law, the railway-telegraph, and a reformed revenue order** together produced a **modern colonial state** — simultaneously **exploitative and, unintentionally, modernising** — whose contradictions bred the very nationalism that would end it.

rows: **Administration**

A **centralised, hierarchical bureaucracy** — the **covenanted Civil Service (ICS)**, rule of law, codified law (Macaulay's **Penal Code 1860**), a professional police (1861) and army; **post-1858 Crown rule** (Government of India Act 1858, Viceroy).
**Revenue & economy**

**Permanent (1793), Ryotwari & Mahalwari** settlements; commercialisation of agriculture; **deindustrialisation** of handicrafts; railways, telegraph, ports built for **extraction & administration** — the drain (HCOI-024).
**Education**
**Macaulay's Minute (1835)** & English education; **Wood's Despatch (1854)** — the education 'magna carta' (universities 1857); a Western-educated middle class emerged — the nationalist vanguard.
**Society & culture**
**Social reform** (abolition of **Sati 1829** — Bentinck/Roy; **Widow Remarriage Act 1856** — Vidyasagar), a modern press, and a colonial 'civilising mission' rhetoric masking economic exploitation.

items: **The modernising instruments (unintended)**: railways, telegraph, English education, a unified legal-administrative framework and the printing press **knit India together** and gave nationalism its language, network and educated leadership — colonial tools turned against the colonisers.

**The exploitative core**: **deindustrialisation** (Indian weavers ruined by machine-made cloth), **recurrent famines** (Bengal 1770, the 1876 & 1896–1900 famines under laissez-faire policy), the **drain**, and racial subordination — the material grievance base.

**The social-reform ferment**: colonial modernity plus indigenous reformers (**Raja Ram Mohan Roy, Vidyasagar, Jyotiba Phule**) produced **legal social reform** (Sati, widow remarriage, age of consent) and a debate on tradition vs modernity — the 19th-century **Renaissance**.

**The AP dimension**: the **Madras Presidency's Ryotwari system (Thomas Munro)**, the coastal-Andhra irrigation works (**Sir Arthur Cotton's Godavari-Krishna anicuts, 1850s**) that transformed deltaic agriculture, and the rise of a Telugu educated class — colonial change had a distinct regional face.

sections.heading: The role of Christian missionaries in colonial India

blocks.text: **Christian missionaries** — enabled after the **Charter Act of 1813** opened India to them — became a **major agent of colonial social and cultural change**. Through **modern schools, colleges, printing presses, hospitals and vernacular scholarship**, they advanced **Western education, social reform and press culture** — even as their **proselytisation provoked reform, revivalism and resistance** among Indians. Their impact, like colonial change itself (HCOI-025), was **double-edged**.

rows: **Education**

Pioneered **modern English & vernacular schools and colleges** (Serampore, Christian colleges); opened education to **lower castes, tribals & women** — but with a conversion aim that spurred Hindu/Muslim educational responses.
**Printing & language**
The **Serampore Press (Carey, Marshman, Ward)** printed Bibles and, crucially, **grammars, dictionaries and vernacular literature** — advancing Bengali, Tamil, **Telugu** and tribal languages.
**Social reform**
Campaigned against **Sati, caste discrimination, female infanticide**; ran **hospitals, orphanages, leprosy & tribal welfare** — real humanitarian work entwined with evangelism.
**Reaction it provoked**

**Socio-religious reform & revival** (Brahmo Samaj, Arya Samaj) partly answered the missionary critique; conversions among tribals/Dalits and cultural anxiety also fed **resentment and 1857 rumours**.

items: **The enabling shift (1813)**: before 1813 the Company **barred missionaries** (fearing unrest); the **Charter Act of 1813 legalised their entry** — thereafter missionary schools and presses multiplied, especially in south India and tribal belts.

**Genuine social contributions**: **female education (the first girls' schools), Dalit & tribal uplift, medical service, and vernacular print** were real and lasting — several modern Indian languages owe early grammars and dictionaries to missionary scholars.

**The provocation-and-response dynamic**: missionary attacks on 'idolatry' and caste **galvanised Hindu reform and revival** (Roy, Dayananda) and sharpened religious identity; fear of forced conversion was among the **rumours behind the 1857 Revolt**.

**The AP dimension**: missionaries were especially active in the **Telugu country and among tribal & Dalit communities** — early **Telugu grammars, dictionaries and printing**, girls' schools and mass education among marginalised groups gave colonial-era Andhra a distinctive missionary imprint (and later a Dalit-Christian social movement).

blocks.text: Exam tip: Present missionaries as a DOUBLE-EDGED agent — real advances in female/Dalit/tribal education, medicine and vernacular print, but proselytisation that provoked reform, revival and 1857 anxieties; the Charter Act of 1813 is the enabling hinge.

prelimsPointers: **Charter Act of 1813** — legalised Christian missionary entry into India (earlier barred by the Company).
**Serampore Trio** — **William Carey, Joshua Marshman, William Ward** — the Serampore Press & vernacular printing/scholarship.
Missionaries pioneered **female education, Dalit & tribal schooling, hospitals and orphanages**.
Missionary critique of caste/idolatry helped spur reform bodies — **Brahmo Samaj, Arya Samaj**.
Fear of forced conversion was among the **rumours contributing to the Revolt of 1857**.
Active in the **Telugu country** — early Telugu grammars/dictionaries, mass education among marginalised groups.
Contributed to abolition campaigns — **Sati, female infanticide** — alongside Indian reformers.
mainsAngles: Assess the double-edged role of Christian missionaries in the social and cultural transformation of colonial India.
Examine the missionary contribution to modern education, especially for women and marginalised communities.
Analyse how missionary activity stimulated Hindu and Muslim socio-religious reform and revival.
Discuss the missionary contribution to vernacular language, print and literature in south India.
Evaluate the missionary imprint on colonial Andhra's educational and social landscape.

glossary.definition: The Act that renewed the EIC charter, ended its trade monopoly (except tea/China) and legally opened India to Christian missionaries.
Carey, Marshman and Ward — Baptist missionaries whose Serampore press pioneered Indian vernacular printing and scholarship.
The active seeking of religious conversions — the missionary aim that provoked Indian reform, revival and resistance.
Printing in Indian languages; missionary presses produced early grammars, dictionaries and literature in Bengali, Tamil and Telugu.
19th-century movements (Brahmo, Arya Samaj) to reform Indian religion and society, partly in response to missionary critique.
